messages.subject: a marketplace for services and coauthorships ?
messages.subject_clean: a marketplace for services and coauthorships ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

motivated by a long email that I got asking for stats help I here share an idea that I had had quite a while ago:  Why not using (among many other ways) these Google group help lists as a marketplace for consulting services in exchange for co-authorships ?

Many of us like to render community service by helping others as much as we can. But sometimes this would require too much of a time commitment and so we can’t do this. I have long thought that people could perhaps send out an advertisement of the kind “Stats consulting help wanted: offer co-authorship in exchange”. I have never seen this and I think some people may feel embarrassed to send out such a call for help. But I really don’t see anything illegitimate in this.  Of course, this would not mean that we should stop giving advice or ask for co-authorships unless we work at least a couple hours…

What do others think ?

Thanks and best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: IPMs - question on modelling the link between count and population size data
messages.subject_clean: IPMs - question on modelling the link between count and population size data
messages.body_plain:
Thank you all very much for your detailed and clear answers. It is much clearer now.

Have a nice day!

Jaume A.

El dia dijous, 28 d’abril de 2022 a les 22:10:06 UTC+2, Michael Schaub va escriure:

> Hi Jaume,
>
> First of all we have to see that the 'observation error' of the IPM is infact the residual error of the IPM, hence it accounts not only for errors in the counts, but also for lack of fit in other parts of the model. Ideally we should decompose the residual error into a component of true observation error and a component of lack of fit. However, with the usual sampling design with a single count each year this decomposition is not possible.
> Having this in mind, it may make sense that the variation of the counts can be in both directions, even if the counts themself are only subject to imperfect detection. Since your counts only have the imperfect detection issue the binomial distribution seems a natural choice, but the detection parameter is not identifiable with a single count. Hence, the remaining options remain therefore the Normal and the Poisson, or the log-Normal. Keep in mind that the estimated population sizes are in this case relative and not absolute.
>
> Best wishes
>
> Michael
> Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von Jaume Adria Badia Boher <jaum...@gmail.com>
> Gesendet: Donnerstag, 28. April 2022 16:19
> An: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
> Betreff: IPMs - question on modelling the link between count and population size data
>
> Hi all!
>
> I have a question about IPM structures that is perhaps basic or has an evident answer. Sorry in advance if this is the case.
>
> I've been reading and working with IPMs lately and my question is specifically about the observation equations that link the observed population counts (i.e. often census data) with the population sizes calculated within the model. That is, for instance, if a normal distribution is chosen to model this link:
>
> Census[t] ~ dnorm(N[age1,t] + N[age2,t], sigma)
>
> where Census[t] are the yearly population counts and N[age,t] are the population size estimations made by the model for different age classes at every year.
>
> or if we choose a poisson distribution:
>
> Census[t] ~ dpois(N[age1,t] + N[age2,t])
>
> All links I can remember to have read between both components of the IPM are calculated using either poisson or normal distributions. However, as I understand, both of these distributions are accounting for both imperfect detection (false negatives) and double counting (false positives).
>  In the case of some study species (mine in this case), there might be different conditions. For instance, in territorial species with strong tenacity to breeding locations throughout their lives and rare-to-no breeding dispersal events, double-counting might be almost impossible or, if present, extremely rare, as individuals will remain in the same location throughout their lives. I am wondering if by using poisson or normal links between both processes in these types of species, we are providing a wrong picture of the uncertainty in the relationship between both processes in the IPM, which may affect the overall performance of the model. In the case that my premise is true, does anybody have an idea about how to deal with this scenario, perhaps by choosing alternative distributions or structures?
>
> Thank you in advance and have a nice day!
>
> Jaume A.
>
>

messages.subject: AHMbook package not on CRAN (temporarily we hope)
messages.subject_clean: AHMbook package not on CRAN (temporarily we hope)
messages.body_plain:
The AHMbook package was removed from CRAN on 4 May 2022. It uses functions in the RandomFields package for several of the spatial data simulations, and RandomFields was removed because it failed CRAN checks.

If you already have AHMbook and RandomFields on your computer, they will continue to work (unless you are running Fedora).

A new version of RandomFields (3.3.18) has been submitted to CRAN, so if all goes well it will reappear on CRAN in the next few days.

This is the second time RandomFields has caused problems, so the next version of AHMbook (0.2.6) will check to see if RandomFields is available, and if not will try to use functions in the fields package instead. This has already been submitted to CRAN.

If you need to install AHMbook in the meantime, you can use
remotes::install_github("mikemeredith/AHMbook")

The fields package cannot cope with large field sizes or high correlations, and many of the examples in the book will not work. In particular, it cannot create the data set analyzed in AHM2 section 9.6.1.2. An example data set is now included in the package as simDynoccSpatialData.

messages.subject: Understanding the influence of predictors with different dimensionality
messages.subject_clean: Understanding the influence of predictors with different dimensionality
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to understand the structure of my open N-mixture model, but I am not entirely sure how predictors with different dimensionality (spatial vs temporal) influence the model.

Model example:

N[s,y] ~ Poisson (lambda[s,y])

log(lambda[s,y]) <- beta0 + beta.A * A[s] +
                                                 beta.B * B[y] +
                                                 beta.C * C[s,y]

Where index "s" represent predictors varying across sites and "y" across years.

How would you interpret the effect of each variable (A, B, and C) on abundance? Is the interpretation of the slopes dependent on the dimensionality of the variable? For example, is A[s] explaining *only* the spatial component of the population estimation?

All the best,

Alejandro

messages.subject_clean: Understanding the influence of predictors with different dimensionality
messages.body_plain:
Dear Alejandro,

yes, exactly as you say. The index of your covariates describes also the dimension along which it can explain variation (Note this is in your case where you organized the data such that a dimension is either space or time. One can write the model for vectorized data and there obviously that space-time dimension information would be lost.).

Best regards --- Marc

messages.subject: psi in data augmentation with subpopulations
messages.subject_clean: psi in data augmentation with subpopulations
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a Q on data augmentation in an occupancy model with subpopulations.

I am helping some otter biologists here in Switzerland better understand their spraint (= crap) surveys in terms of detection probability. One data set is from a tripled survey with an expert, a trained volunteer, and a search dog doing the same stretch of river one after the other and recording every spraint found. This is repeated in two winters and then they are interested in contrasting p among 4 mutually exclusive river 'naturalness categories'. Hence, I am fitting a closed-population  model implemented as an occupancy model, where I distinguish 8 subpopulations (winter x category), for which I do separate DA. (I know I could do the Royle, Link, Converse ~ 2012 thing but that hurts my brain more so I do it the pedestrian and clumsy way.)

Now I am a little lost in seeing the difference between a model that has a single DA parameter psi and one for which psi is different for each subpopulation. Here are the estimates of spraint population sizes (NU) per subpopulation in a model with a single psi (psi and constant p also shown):

p          0.422  0.028   0.367   0.422   0.477    FALSE 1 1.000  4000

And here they are with different psi estimated for each:

psiU[1,1]   0.111  0.035   0.052   0.108   0.190    FALSE 1 1.001  1500

NU[2,1]    16.599  2.190  13.000  16.000  21.000    FALSE 1 1.007   438

NU[1,2]     9.069  1.667   7.000   9.000  13.000    FALSE 1 1.000  1500

Hey Marc, I think the major difference is that the variances of the population sizes are forced to be essentially the same with a single psi.  If you allow psi to vary by subpopulation, the variance scales more with population size.

Dear Dan,

thanks ! And what would you consider to be more adequate ?

I have also noticed that when I let psi to vary by subpopulation, then the combined detection probability (P) across the three surveys is the usual "binomial" function of the per-survey p, while when I have a single psi, they are not and all over the place. So I like the separate-psi model much better.

Here are the estimates of per-survey p and combined P for each subpopulation when I fit a single psi.

messages.body_plain:
I definitely think the latter is better, allowing psi to vary by subpopulation.  Suppose you could make it hierarchical too, given the 8 subpopulations.

One analogy is a closed capture-recapture model with sex.  The proper approach is either you fix the sex for your augmented individuals and allow sex-specific psi (psi_f, psi_m), or you could have a single psi and sex is assigned a probability distribution (pr_m) for the augmented individuals.  In either case, you are estimating 2 probabilities.  If you kept a single probability for psi and fixed the sex for the augmented individuals with no probability distribution, you are constraining the model in a potentially undesirable way.

Admittedly, I'm shooting from the hip here... :)

From: Hebblewhite, Mark <Mark.Heb...@mso.umt.edu>

Subject: Post-doctoral research position on Ungulate spatial/population ecology at University of Montana

Dear Colleagues,

Please redistribute in your departments for prospective Post-doctoral candidates.  THANK YOU

Post-doctoral Research Associate: Spatial and Population Ecology of Large Herbivores in a Changing World

I am recruiting a Postdoctoral Research Associate (PDRA) to join our lab in summer 2022 for 2-3 years focused on developing innovative, independent-lead research on the spatial and population ecology of barrenground caribou in the Arctic as part of an NSF-funded Navigating the New Arctic (NNA) project:  Fate of the Caribou: from local knowledge to range-wide dynamics in the changing Arctic. <https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2127272> The PDRA will also have opportunities to develop independent research on my NSF-funded Long-term Research in Environmental Biology (LTREB)  Ya Ha Tinda elk research project <https://www.cfc.umt.edu/research/heblab/projects/yaha-tinda-elk.php>, amongst the world’s longest-running studies of elk.

The successful PDRA will work with an interagency team based at SUNY-ESF lead by  Eliezer Gurarie <https://eligurarie.github.io/>, with  Scott Goetz <https://directory.nau.edu/person/sjg326> and  Logan Berner <https://goetzlab.rc.nau.edu/index.php/people/> at Northern Arizona University,  Bill Fagan <https://science.umd.edu/biology/faganlab/> at U. of Maryland, Anne Gunn (former Govt NWT), as well as state and federal caribou management agencies in Alaska and Canada, and indigenous groups and governments throughout Northwestern North America's Arctic region. In our Ya Ha Tinda work, the PDRA will collaborate with PhD students in our Lab and co-PI  Evelyn Merrill <https://grad.biology.ualberta.ca/merrill/> (Emeritus) at the U. of Alberta, as well as with Parks Canada managers.

The position is based in the  Ungulate Ecology Lab <https://www.cfc.umt.edu/research/heblab/>, within the  Wildlife Biology Program <https://www.cfc.umt.edu/wbio/> in the  W.A. Franke College of Forestry and Conservation <https://www.cfc.umt.edu/> (FCFC) with opportunities for collaboration on a variety of projects, graduate teaching, and field work.

Qualifications (required): PhD in wildlife biology, ecology, conservation biology, or related field; Demonstrated experience with statistical and spatial modeling, programming, R, GIS analyses, remote sensing, and scientific writing are core qualifications for this position; outstanding work ethic; exceptional quantitative skills and motivation; excellence in oral and written scientific publications; experience with analyses of GPS movement data from animals; excellence in communication and interpersonal skills; demonstrated experience working collaboratively with wildlife management agencies; (preferred qualifications); experience working with Indigenous knowledge, First Nations or co-management boards; field experience in large herbivores preferred; field experience in the subarctic or arctic preferred.  As well as a sense of humor!

How to apply: Send cover letter summarizing interest and relevant experience, resume/CV, unofficial transcripts, GRE scores, and contact information for 3 references (including phone and email – letters not required at initial screening stage) to Dr. Mark Hebblewhite (mark.heb...@umontana.edu), Wildlife Biology Program, W. A. Franke College of Forestry and Conservation, University of Montana, Missoula, MT, USA, 59812. Position will start in late Summer or early Fall 2022. University of Montana Wildlife Biology Program application deadline is ~ June 15 or until a suitable candidate is found. Top candidates will be contacted for interviews and to apply through UM’s human resources portal.

Position Details: Annual salary starting at $50,000/year including benefits, retirement package and health care. NSF-Career Work Life Balance <https://www.nsf.gov/career-life-balance/> family leave supplemental funding potentially available, pending additional funding. Professional development, national and international (Canada) travel, training, and teaching opportunities. Position preferred to be based physically at University of Montana in Missoula.

University of Montana and Missoula: The University of Montana is one of the nation’s outstanding public research (R1) universities, committed to liberal arts education, research, and strong professional programs. UM is located in Missoula, a northern Rocky Mountain city located between Yellowstone and Glacier National Parks. Missoula boasts abundant recreational opportunities with a blend of small-town charm and urban sophistication. Scientists and students have access to FCFC’s Lubrecht Experimental Forest and Bandy Experimental Ranch, the Flathead Lake Biological Station, and the Boone and Crockett Club’s Theodore Roosevelt Memorial Ranch. In addition, there is a strong non-University research community in the surrounding area including the Rocky Mountain Research Station, several non-profit groups, tribal, state and federal scientists (e.g., USGS, USFS).

messages.subject: Selecting between state categorizations
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm interested in others' thoughts on a question perhaps equally philosophical as statistical.

It's common to use multi-state models to compare demographic rates between different sites, represented as states in the model.

But sometimes,  there are multiple possibilities for how to divide continuous space into discrete states, which may seem a priori equally valid: for example, should two breeding colonies on the same island be treated as a single state, or two?

I'm wondering what approaches people use to determine whether adding an additional state is worthwhile, or two choose between different categorizations. The question seems distinct from other types of model selection (e.g. adding a covariate, or changing a distribution), as the response variables are necessarily different.

Many thanks,

Josh Nightingale
